items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.

items.title: Hindu deities are often understood as manifestations of one Brahman
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions; the Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names'
There is only one god — Brahma alone

items.reveal:
The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical mapping of cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine — Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Sikhism was founded in 1469 by Guru Nanak
items.claim: What was Guru Nanak's central teaching?

options.text: A synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism

One God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), remembrance of God (naam japna) — rejecting caste, ritualism and religious exclusivism of his time
A purely philosophical movement with no religious claims

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib (now in Pakistan), Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499. After emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with this affirmation.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.
